betaSandwich: Example Using the SCorSandwich, SCorSqSandwich, PCorSandwich, DeltaRSqSandwich, and FSqSandwich Functions

Ivan Jacob Agaloos Pesigan

Source: vignettes/example-es-sandwich.Rmd
example-es-sandwich.Rmd

Confidence intervals for semipartial correlations, squared semipartial correlations, squared partial correlations, the improvement in R-squared, and Cohen’s f-squared are generated using the SCorSandwich(), SCorSqSandwich(), PCorSandwich(), DeltaRSqSandwich(), and FSqSandwich() functions from the betaSandwich package. In this example, we use the data set and the model used in betaSandwich: Example Using the BetaHC Function.

library(package = betaSandwich)
df <- betaSandwich::nas1982

Effect sizes

Let \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\ast} be the vector of standardized slopes, \boldsymbol{R}_{x} the correlation matrix of the regressors, r^{jj} the jth diagonal element of \boldsymbol{R}_{x}^{-1}, n the sample size, and k the number of parameters of the regression model, including the intercept. Each effect size below is a function g\left( \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\ast} \right) of the standardized parameters. Its sampling variance is approximated by the delta method,

\widehat{\operatorname{var}} \left( \hat{g} \right) = \boldsymbol{J}_{g} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\ast}} \boldsymbol{J}_{g}^{\prime},

where \boldsymbol{J}_{g} is the Jacobian of g and \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\ast}} is the sampling covariance matrix from BetaHC(), BetaADF(), or BetaN() (Yuan & Chan, 2011). The three functions differ in the estimator of the asymptotic covariance matrix of the sample covariances. BetaN() assumes multivariate normality (Browne, 1984). BetaADF() uses sample fourth moments and requires only that they exist, but it is noisy in small samples (Browne, 1984; Jones & Waller, 2015). BetaHC() keeps the normal-theory model for the regressors but replaces the assumption of constant error variance with the squared residuals of the cases (HC0 to HC5) (Cribari-Neto, 2004; Dudgeon, 2017; MacKinnon & White, 1985; White, 1980), and it is recommended in most situations. Confidence intervals are \hat{g} \pm z_{1 - \alpha / 2} \, \widehat{\mathrm{se}} \left( \hat{g} \right).

R-squared and adjusted R-squared (RSqSandwich())

R^{2} = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\ast\prime} \boldsymbol{R}_{x} \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\ast}, \quad \bar{R}^{2} = 1 - \left( 1 - R^{2} \right) \frac{n - 1}{n - k}.

R^{2} is the proportion of the variance of the outcome explained by the regressors. \bar{R}^{2} corrects R^{2} for the number of regressors.

Semipartial correlation (SCorSandwich())

sr_{j} = \frac{\beta^{\ast}_{j}}{\sqrt{r^{jj}}} = \beta^{\ast}_{j} \sqrt{1 - R^{2}_{j \cdot -j}},

where R^{2}_{j \cdot -j} is the R-squared from regressing regressor j on the other regressors. It is the correlation between the outcome and the part of regressor j that is not explained by the other regressors. Because 1 / r^{jj} = 1 - R^{2}_{j \cdot -j}, sr_{j} shrinks toward zero as regressor j becomes more redundant with the other regressors, even when \beta^{\ast}_{j} does not.

Improvement in R-squared (DeltaRSqSandwich())

\Delta R^{2}_{j} = R^{2} - R^{2}_{-j} = sr^{2}_{j}.

It is the change in R^{2} when regressor j is added last, the proportion of the variance of the outcome that regressor j alone accounts for.

Squared semipartial correlation interval (SCorSqSandwich())

The interval \left[ l, u \right] of the signed sr_{j} is squared as a set. The result is \left[ l^{2}, u^{2} \right] if 0 < l, \left[ u^{2}, l^{2} \right] if u < 0, and \left[ 0, \max \left( l^{2}, u^{2} \right) \right] if the interval contains zero. This is not the delta-method interval of DeltaRSqSandwich().

Squared partial correlation (PCorSandwich())

pr^{2}_{j} = \frac{sr^{2}_{j}}{1 - R^{2} + sr^{2}_{j}}.

It is the proportion of the variance of the outcome not explained by the other regressors that is explained by regressor j.

Cohen’s f-squared and local f-squared (FSqSandwich())

f^{2} = \frac{R^{2}}{1 - R^{2}}, \quad f^{2}_{j} = \frac{sr^{2}_{j}}{1 - R^{2}}.

By convention (Cohen, 1988), values of about 0.02, 0.15, and 0.35 are small, medium, and large effects.

Differences of standardized slopes (DiffBetaSandwich())

\beta^{\ast}_{j} - \beta^{\ast}_{l}.

It compares the standardized effects of regressors j and l on the same scale.

Effect sizes near zero

\beta^{\ast}_{j} and sr_{j} are signed and have no boundary at zero. R^{2}, \Delta R^{2}_{j}, pr^{2}_{j}, and f^{2}_{j} cannot be negative. When the population value is zero, the gradient of the squared effect sizes is zero, the first-order delta-method variance vanishes, and a symmetric Wald interval is not justified. Near zero, the sampling distribution remains skewed and bounded in finite samples, and the interval can extend below zero. An interval for sr_{j} can therefore behave well where the interval for sr^{2}_{j} does not. SCorSqSandwich() respects the bound by squaring the interval of sr_{j} as a set.

Fit the regression model using the lm() function. 

object <- stats::lm(formula = QUALITY ~ NARTIC + PCTGRT + PCTSUPP, data = df)

Estimate the standardized regression slopes and the corresponding sampling covariance matrix.

Multivariate Normal-Theory Approach 

std_mvn <- BetaN(object = object)

Asymptotic Distribution-Free Approach 

std_adf <- BetaADF(object = object)

HC3 

std_hc3 <- BetaHC(object = object, type = "hc3")

Semipartial correlations

The semipartial correlation of regressor j is sr_{j} = \beta^{\ast}_{j} / \sqrt{\left[ \boldsymbol{R}_{x}^{-1} \right]_{jj}}, the correlation between the outcome and the part of regressor j that is not explained by the other regressors.

summary(object = SCorSandwich(object = std_hc3, alpha = 0.05))
#> Call:
#> SCorSandwich(object = std_hc3, alpha = 0.05)
#> 
#> Semipartial correlations with HC3 standard errors:
#>            est     se      z      p   2.5%  97.5%
#> NARTIC  0.4312 0.0794 5.4303 0.0000 0.2755 0.5868
#> PCTGRT  0.3430 0.0789 4.3468 0.0000 0.1883 0.4977
#> PCTSUPP 0.2385 0.0783 3.0465 0.0023 0.0851 0.3919

Squared semipartial correlations

The SCorSqSandwich() function squares the signed-semipartial interval as a set. If the signed interval contains zero, the lower limit of the squared interval is zero. Writing the signed interval as \left[ l, u \right], the squared interval is \left[ l^{2}, u^{2} \right] if 0 < l, \left[ u^{2}, l^{2} \right] if u < 0, and \left[ 0, \max \left( l^{2}, u^{2} \right) \right] otherwise. The function returns a data frame with the estimate and the confidence limits.

SCorSqSandwich(object = std_hc3, level = 0.95)
#>               est       lower     upper
#> NARTIC  0.1858925 0.075919679 0.3442987
#> PCTGRT  0.1176542 0.035474114 0.2476748
#> PCTSUPP 0.0568722 0.007234428 0.1535875

Squared partial correlations

The squared partial correlation is pr^{2}_{j} = sr^{2}_{j} / \left( 1 - R^{2} + sr^{2}_{j} \right), the proportion of the variance of the outcome not explained by the other regressors that is explained by regressor j.

summary(object = PCorSandwich(object = std_hc3, alpha = 0.05))
#> Call:
#> PCorSandwich(object = std_hc3, alpha = 0.05)
#> 
#> Squared partial correlations with HC3 standard errors:
#>            est     se      z      p    2.5%  97.5%
#> NARTIC  0.4874 0.1095 4.4532 0.0000  0.2729 0.7020
#> PCTGRT  0.3757 0.1156 3.2500 0.0012  0.1491 0.6023
#> PCTSUPP 0.2254 0.1277 1.7647 0.0776 -0.0249 0.4757

Improvement in R-squared

The improvement in R-squared is \Delta R^{2}_{j} = R^{2} - R^{2}_{-j} = sr^{2}_{j}, the decrease in R^{2} when regressor j is removed from the model.

summary(object = DeltaRSqSandwich(object = std_hc3, alpha = 0.05))
#> Call:
#> DeltaRSqSandwich(object = std_hc3, alpha = 0.05)
#> 
#> Improvement in R-squared with HC3 standard errors:
#>            est     se      z      p    2.5%  97.5%
#> NARTIC  0.1859 0.0685 2.7151 0.0066  0.0517 0.3201
#> PCTGRT  0.1177 0.0541 2.1734 0.0298  0.0116 0.2238
#> PCTSUPP 0.0569 0.0373 1.5233 0.1277 -0.0163 0.1300

Cohen’s f-squared and local f-squared

Cohen’s f-squared is f^{2} = R^{2} / \left( 1 - R^{2} \right) and the local f-squared of regressor j is f^{2}_{j} = sr^{2}_{j} / \left( 1 - R^{2} \right). By convention, values of about 0.02, 0.15, and 0.35 are small, medium, and large effects.

summary(object = FSqSandwich(object = std_hc3, alpha = 0.05))
#> Call:
#> FSqSandwich(object = std_hc3, alpha = 0.05)
#> 
#> Cohen's f-squared (fsq) and local f-squared with HC3 standard errors:
#>            est     se      z      p    2.5%  97.5%
#> fsq     4.1158 1.5009 2.7422 0.0061  1.1741 7.0575
#> NARTIC  0.9510 0.4166 2.2825 0.0225  0.1344 1.7676
#> PCTGRT  0.6019 0.2967 2.0288 0.0425  0.0204 1.1834
#> PCTSUPP 0.2909 0.2128 1.3670 0.1716 -0.1262 0.7081

Extracting estimates, sampling covariance matrices, and confidence intervals

The coef(), vcov(), and confint() methods work on the objects returned by the effect size functions.

scor <- SCorSandwich(object = std_hc3)
stats::coef(object = scor)
#>    NARTIC    PCTGRT   PCTSUPP 
#> 0.4311525 0.3430075 0.2384789
stats::vcov(object = scor)
#>                NARTIC        PCTGRT       PCTSUPP
#> NARTIC   0.0063040434 -0.0002532449 -0.0004374935
#> PCTGRT  -0.0002532449  0.0062268718 -0.0010139363
#> PCTSUPP -0.0004374935 -0.0010139363  0.0061275595
stats::confint(object = scor, level = 0.95)
#>              2.5 %    97.5 %
#> NARTIC  0.27553526 0.5867697
#> PCTGRT  0.18834573 0.4976693
#> PCTSUPP 0.08505544 0.3919024

Comparing covariance estimators 

stats::confint(object = DeltaRSqSandwich(object = std_mvn), level = 0.95)
#>                2.5 %    97.5 %
#> NARTIC   0.055421734 0.3163632
#> PCTGRT   0.017881671 0.2174267
#> PCTSUPP -0.008779331 0.1225237
stats::confint(object = DeltaRSqSandwich(object = std_adf), level = 0.95)
#>                2.5 %    97.5 %
#> NARTIC   0.072394224 0.2993907
#> PCTGRT   0.025067308 0.2102410
#> PCTSUPP -0.008691312 0.1224357
stats::confint(object = DeltaRSqSandwich(object = std_hc3), level = 0.95)
#>               2.5 %    97.5 %
#> NARTIC   0.05170296 0.3200820
#> PCTGRT   0.01155384 0.2237545
#> PCTSUPP -0.01630434 0.1300487
